question: What happens to Ahaziah, whom does he send to inquire of, and how does he recognize Elijah from the messengers' description?
The verb דָּרַשׁ (darash, “inquire, seek”) is at the center of the accusation: what question does Elijah repeat three times, and what does it reveal about the king's problem?
What sets the third captain apart from the first two, and how do you read the fire that falls on the other hundred men?
“Is there no God in Israel?”: when you are in crisis, to whom or what do you turn first?
How many times does Elijah ask Elisha to stay behind, and what is Elisha's answer in each place?
The verb לָקַח (laqach, “take”) describes what the LORD will do with Elijah: why do the prophets comment on it and Elisha asks them to be quiet?
What does the request for a “double portion” of Elijah's spirit mean, and how do the cloak and the crossing of the Jordan confirm the succession?
The episode of the bears is one of the hardest in the book: what does the text actually narrate, and how have readers of different traditions sought to understand it?
Elisha asks “Where is the LORD, the God of Elijah?” right after losing his master: how do you seek God's presence when an important reference in your life is gone?
Why does Joram go to war against Moab, who joins him and what problem arises in the wilderness of Edom?
The water, מַיִם (mayim), first runs out, then fills the valley and finally deceives the Moabites: how does the same element change roles throughout the chapter?
Why does Elisha treat Joram so harshly and agree to speak only because of Jehoshaphat?
The chapter ends with the king of Moab sacrificing his son and Israel withdrawing: what does this strange and tragic ending leave unexplained?
The order to cut down every good tree and stop up the springs describes a war that destroys the land's future: what limits should faith place on destruction in today's conflicts?
What is the situation of the prophet's widow, and what instructions does Elisha give her about the jars?
What does the Shunammite woman do for Elisha without asking for anything, and how does she respond when he offers something in return?
The Shunammite answers only שָׁלוֹם (shalom, “peace, all is well”) to her husband and to Gehazi, even with her son dead: what does this word reveal about her at that moment?
Twenty loaves seem little for a hundred people, and still there is some left: what small resource of yours do you hesitate to offer because you think it will make no difference?
Who is Naaman, what is his problem, and who gives him the idea of seeking the prophet in Israel?
The word נָבִיא (navi', “prophet”) appears on the lips of the captive girl, of Elisha and of the servants: what is needed for Naaman to discover “that there is a prophet in Israel”?
Why does Elisha's simple instruction anger Naaman, and what do his servants make him realize?
What does Gehazi do after Elisha refuses the gifts, and why is his lie judged so severely?
A girl taken captive cares about her master's healing: how can you do good to someone who has power over you, or has even harmed you?
What happens to the borrowed axe head, and why does it worry the prophet who was using it so much?
The verb פָּקַח (paqach, “open the eyes”) appears twice, with opposite effects: what does the young man come to see, and what do the Arameans discover when their eyes are opened?
Why does Elisha have the enemies fed instead of killed, and what result does this bring?
“Those who are with us are more than those who are with them”: in what situation of fear would you like to see what you are not seeing?
How do the four lepers reason before going to the Aramean camp, and what do they find there?
The שַׁעַר (sha‘ar, “gate” of the city) appears in the announcement of prices, in the place of the lepers and in the officer's death: what happens in each of these scenes at the gate?
What does the officer's doubt reveal, and why does the text repeat at the end his phrase about “windows in heaven”?
“This is a day of good news, and we are keeping silent”: what good news or good gift have you kept only to yourself?
Why does the Shunammite leave the land for seven years, and how does she recover her house and land on returning?
The verb חָיָה (chayah, “live, recover”) passes from the Shunammite to Ben-hadad's question: how does Hazael twist Elisha's answer about “living” and “dying”?
Why does Elisha weep before Hazael, and what does this scene say about the prophet who sees his people's future suffering?
Why is Judah not destroyed although Jehoram follows the house of Ahab, and to what image of the book does the “lamp” refer?
The Shunammite appears at the very moment Gehazi is telling her story to the king: how do you usually interpret coincidences that change the course of a situation?
How is Jehu anointed king, and how do his companions react when he tells them what happened?
The question “Is there peace?” is repeated several times: what answer does Jehu give, and why does he say there can be no peace?
The דָּם (dam, “blood”) of the prophets and of Naboth is remembered in the anointing and in Joram's death: why is Joram's body thrown precisely onto Naboth's property?
Jezebel dies without anyone being able to recognize her body: what do you think of the way the text narrates the end of someone powerful who oppressed others?
How does Jehu eliminate Ahab's seventy sons without laying a hand on them directly?
The verb עָבַד (‘avad, “serve”) appears in Jehu's trap, “Jehu will serve him much”: what does the use of lies and cunning reveal about the way he fights Baal?
Jehu destroys Baal but keeps the calves of Bethel and Dan: what does this half-reform show about him and about the book's criterion?
Jehu invites Jehonadab to see his “zeal for the LORD”: how does this zeal compare with Elijah's zeal in 1 Kings 19, and what questions does it raise about violence in God's name?
Jehu “was not careful to walk in the law of the LORD with all his heart”: in what do you run the risk of fighting others' errors without reviewing your own?
What does Athaliah do on learning of her son's death, and how does Joash escape?
Jehoiada's plan is organized around the שַׁבָּת (shabbat, “Sabbath”) and the change of guard: why is this day used to protect the boy king?
What gestures mark the coronation of Joash, and why does Jehoiada make a covenant involving the LORD, the king and the people?
Jehosheba risks her life to hide a child for six years: who, discreetly, protected your future when you could not defend yourself?
What plan does Joash make to repair the temple, and why does it not work in the first years?
The word בֶּדֶק (bedeq, “breach, damage to repair”) appears several times: what change in the way money is handled finally allows the breaches of the temple to be repaired?
The text says Joash did what was right “all the days Jehoiada the priest instructed him”: what does this qualification suggest about him and about the rest of his reign?
Those in charge of the work did not have to give an account “because they dealt faithfully”: in what area of your life could you be someone worthy of this kind of trust?
What situation is Israel in under Jehoahaz, and what happens when he prays to the LORD?
Elisha calls the arrow shot through the window “the arrow of victory,” using חֵץ (chets, “arrow”): what does this gesture, with the prophet's hand on the king's, communicate?
Why is Elisha angry when the king strikes the ground only three times, and what does this say about the king's disposition?
What is the meaning, at the end of the chapter, of the dead man who revives on touching Elisha's bones, and of the reminder of the covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob?
The king stops too soon: in what project or prayer have you been content with little, when you could have persisted more?
What challenge does Amaziah make to Jehoash of Israel, how does Jehoash respond and what is the result?
Amaziah does not kill the sons of the assassins, for each one “will die” (מוּת, mut) for his own sin: what principle of the law of Moses does he follow, and why does the narrator highlight it?
Jeroboam II does what is evil, and yet the LORD saves Israel through him: what reason does the text give for this?
The fable of the thistle and the cedar warns against pride after a victory: at what moment has a success of yours led you to risk more than you should?
How many kings pass through Israel's throne in this chapter, and how do most of them end?
The verb סוּר (sur, “turn away, be removed”) is repeated in fixed formulas: what is never removed in Judah, and from what do the kings of Israel never turn away?
Why does Menahem pay a thousand talents to the king of Assyria, and what does this decision foreshadow for the future of the northern kingdom?
Azariah spends the rest of his life isolated because of leprosy, while his son governs: how do you see the worth of someone who has lost his position but is still present?
What threat does Ahaz face, and to whom does he turn for help?
The מִזְבֵּחַ (mizbeach, “altar”) copied from Damascus takes the place of the bronze altar: what does this exchange reveal about Ahaz's priorities?
Ahaz declares himself “your servant and your son” before the king of Assyria: what contrast is there between this phrase and the identity of the kings of David's house?
Ahaz changes even the structure of the temple “on account of the king of Assyria”: in what have you adjusted your convictions to please those who have power?
What political mistake by Hoshea provokes Assyria's reaction, and what happens to Samaria and the people?
What explanation does the narrator give for the fall of the northern kingdom, and why does he interrupt the story to make this long assessment?
The verb יָרֵא (yare', “fear”) appears many times in the account of the peoples brought to Samaria: what does it mean to “fear the LORD” and at the same time serve other gods?
According to verse 13, how did the LORD warn Israel and Judah before the exile, and what kept the people from listening?
“They feared the LORD, but they also served their own gods”: what divided loyalties do you recognize in your own life?
What reforms does Hezekiah carry out, and what does he do with Moses' bronze serpent?
The verb בָּטַח (batach, “trust”) runs through the Rabshakeh's speech: in what, according to him, could Hezekiah be trusting, and why is each option discredited?
Why do Hezekiah's envoys ask the Rabshakeh to speak in Aramaic, and why are the people ordered not to answer?
Hezekiah destroys a sacred object from the past because it had become an object of worship: is there something good in your life that has ended up taking God's place?
What does Hezekiah do on hearing the Rabshakeh's words, and what answer does he receive from Isaiah?
What does Hezekiah do with the letters, and what reason does he give God for asking for the salvation of Jerusalem?

The verb חָרַף (charaf, “taunt, defy”) describes the words of the king of Assyria against “the living God”: what other taunt, in 1 Samuel 17, uses the same language, and what do the two stories have in common?
What picture of the future does the sign given to Hezekiah offer to the remnant of Judah?
Hezekiah “spread out the letter before the LORD”: what letter, news or threat would you need to lay before God in prayer?
What news does Isaiah bring to the sick Hezekiah, what does Hezekiah do, and how does the answer change?
The צֵל (tsel, “shadow”) that goes back ten steps is the sign Hezekiah asks for: why does he consider it harder for the shadow to go back than to go forward?
What does Hezekiah show the envoys from Babylon, and why does Isaiah react with such a grave announcement?
Hezekiah takes comfort that there will be peace “in my lifetime”: how do you weigh the consequences of your choices for the generations that come after?
What does Manasseh rebuild, introduce and place even inside the house of the LORD?

The word רַע (ra‘, “evil”) is repeated in the evaluation of Manasseh and in the announcement of punishment: what relationship does the chapter establish between the evil committed and the evil that will come upon Jerusalem?
What do the images of the measuring line of Samaria and the dish wiped clean and turned upside down, applied to Jerusalem, mean?
Manasseh filled Jerusalem with “innocent blood”: what injustices against the innocent in your city today can you not ignore?
What task does Josiah order to be done in the temple, and what does Hilkiah find during the work?
The סֵפֶר (sefer, “book”) of the law passes from hand to hand until it reaches the king: why does a forgotten book provoke such a strong reaction in Josiah?
Why is it significant that the prophetess Huldah is consulted, and what does she announce for the people and for the king?
Josiah's heart “was tender” on hearing the word: how do you react when a biblical text confronts something in your life?
What does Josiah do with the book that was found before all the people, and what commitment is made?
The word בָּמָה (bamah, “high place, shrine”) appears throughout the reform: which high places are destroyed, and which of them dated back to Solomon and Jeroboam?
How does Josiah's action at Bethel fulfill what the man of God had announced in 1 Kings 13, and why are his bones spared?
Josiah is the most praised king, and still the punishment of Judah is not revoked: how should we understand this tension in the text?
The reform ends with the celebration of the Passover as never before: what practice of memory and celebration would help renew your faith?
Who is taken to Babylon in the first deportation, and who remains in the land?
To what causes does the narrator attribute the invasion of Judah, and why does he mention Manasseh and the innocent blood again?
The word גּוֹלָה (golah, “exile, group of captives”) enters the story here: what concrete losses, besides the land, do the people suffer when they are taken away?
Only “the poorest people of the land” are left behind: how do you see those who are left aside when the structures of a society collapse?
How does the siege of Jerusalem end, and what happens to Zedekiah and his sons?
The נְחֹשֶׁת (nechoshet, “bronze”) of the pillars and the sea, described with pride in 1 Kings 7, is broken up and carried off: what effect does this detailed memory have in the midst of destruction?
What attempt at a new beginning arises with Gedaliah at Mizpah, and why does it fail?
Why do the books of Kings end with Jehoiachin released from prison and eating at the king of Babylon's table? What kind of hope does this ending leave?
The book ends with a small sign of favor in the midst of exile: what small sign of hope can you recognize in a difficult period of your life?
